clue.text: Vigorously hearty team members having a drink

parts.note: backs are players in the rear positions of a rugby or football team
an animal lapping water is drinking it with its tongue

explanation.surface: Sports players out for a pint, being boisterously matey with one another.
explanation.definitionFit: A back-slapping manner is loudly and effusively jovial, the hearty greeting of a pat on the back.

clue.text: In outskirts of Bhopal, brutal altercation

indicators.note: the brutal word is placed in, between the two edge letters of the city name
the outskirts of a word are its outer letters, here of the city name Bhopal

parts.note: raw can mean harsh or brutal, as in raw violence

explanation.surface: A violent quarrel breaking out on the edge of the Indian city of Bhopal.
explanation.definitionFit: A brawl is a rough, noisy fight or quarrel, a physical altercation.

clue.text: Bird with a ring, displaying elation

parts.note: a cock is a male bird, especially a rooster
a hoop is a circular band or ring

explanation.surface: A bird wearing a ring, perhaps a tagged pigeon, looking very pleased with itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Cock-a-hoop is an idiom for being jubilant or exultant, so it describes someone showing great delight.

clue.text: Dishonest dealings rare in talented singers?

definitions.meaning: underhand or unscrupulous methods in business
read literally, the habit of singing above pitch, which gifted vocalists seldom do

explanation.surface: A complaint that crooked business is seldom found among gifted vocalists.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the phrase literally: a singer who goes sharp is off pitch, and good singers rarely get into that habit.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names cheating or deceitful conduct in trade, while the literal reading is a vocal fault of going above pitch.

clue.text: Part of speech of vicar brought up in bad development

indicators.note: the turned vicar word goes inside the rearranged letters
a development of the word bad is a new arrangement of its letters
in a down clue, brought up means the word is written from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: Rev, short for Reverend, is the title of a vicar

explanation.surface: A grammar point is made of a clergyman being mentioned in a sorry turn of events.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'brought up' means written upwards. Rev, the vicar's title, is the usual crossword clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb is one of the grammatical word classes, a word modifying a verb or adjective.

clue.text: Peeved informer about to retire…

parts.note: put out means annoyed or irritated
a grass is British slang for a police informer

explanation.surface: An irritated snitch who is about to leave work for good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is padding that leads into the next clue; 'to' is used as it stands. GRASS is British slang for one who tells tales to the police.
explanation.definitionFit: To put out to grass is an idiom for pensioning off a horse or worker, making them retire.

clue.text: …and not nervous of retirement at first

indicators.note: the opening letter of each of the three words before it is taken

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: and someone who has no worries about leaving work.
explanation.definitionFit: The conjunction joins a further negative alternative, as in neither this nor that.

clue.text: Small photo capturing start of county cricket, for example

indicators.note: the small photo word holds the next letter inside it

parts.note: an inset is a small picture placed within a larger one

indicators.note: only the first letter of county is used

explanation.surface: A snapshot taken at a county cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests county cricket, the English inter-county game, but cricket is the chirping insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A cricket is a chirping jumping creature with six legs, one example of that class of arthropod.

clue.text: Part of circle about to retire in Ghanaian port

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the combined letters are read backwards

parts.note: an arc is a section of a circle's circumference
ca, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A geometry fragment withdrawing to a West African harbour town.
explanation.definitionFit: Accra is the capital of Ghana and a seaport on the Gulf of Guinea.

clue.text: Long-serving surgeon managed to save energy

indicators.note: saving something means keeping it safe inside, so the energy letter is held within

parts.note: a vet is an animal surgeon
ran means managed, as one runs a business
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: An experienced surgeon somehow kept his strength up.
explanation.definitionFit: A veteran has served for a long time, so the noun works adjectivally as long-serving.

clue.text: Tragic king cut down in grassy area

indicators.note: cutting down means shortening, here losing the final letter

parts.note: King Lear is the title character of Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: A tragic monarch slain in a meadow.
explanation.definitionFit: A lea is a poetic word for a meadow or open pasture.

clue.text: Spiny rodent's meat talked of up in Edinburgh originally

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: the meat word is heard spoken, giving a different spelling

parts.note: pork is pig meat

indicators.note: the first letter of Edinburgh is taken

explanation.surface: A prickly creature's flesh being discussed up in the Scottish capital.
explanation.definitionFit: A porcupine is a large rodent covered in protective quills.

clue.text: Self-same dialect in new form

indicators.note: giving the letters a new form means rearranging them

explanation.surface: A regional way of speaking reshaped yet somehow unchanged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new form' rearranges DIALECT together with IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-same means the very same, exactly alike, a synonym for identical.

clue.text: Meal served by a number (about fifty?)

indicators.note: the number word goes about, around, the fifty letter

parts.note: four is a number
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Food served by a group of people, perhaps around fifty of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Meal also means ground grain, a coarse powder close in sense to flour.

clue.text: Painting Al's left in the open air

indicators.note: having left means gone away, so his letters drop out

parts.note: al fresco means outdoors
Al's here is short for Al has; Al is a man's name

explanation.surface: A man called Al leaves his artwork outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A fresco is a mural painted onto wet plaster.

clue.text: Negotiate terms for an excursion, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to bargain or discuss conditions with another party
an outing given as a special pleasure is one example of an indulgence

explanation.surface: Bargaining over the conditions for a day trip.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to parley over conditions, and the noun is a special delight such as an outing.

clue.text: One way to get involved in brother's restaurant

indicators.note: being involved in something means being inside it

parts.note: bro is short for brother
I is the Roman numeral one
St is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A route into the family business: the brother's eatery.
explanation.definitionFit: A bistro is a small, informal restaurant, originally French.

clue.text: Anticipate gin flowing in the club

parts.note: to expect is to anticipate

indicators.note: flowing letters move freely into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Looking forward to the gin pouring at a members' club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flowing' rearranges GIN to ING. 'In the club' is British slang for pregnant, not a place.
explanation.definitionFit: In the club is British slang for pregnant, which is what expecting means of a mother-to-be.

clue.text: Young child going to and fro

definitions.note: a small child, and the word reads the same in either direction

indicators.note: going both ways means the word reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: a small child, and the word reads the same in either direction

explanation.surface: A toddler running back and forth.
explanation.definitionFit: A tot is an informal word for a small child.

clue.text: Article about Italian wine tax no longer levied

indicators.note: the article goes about, around, the wine letters

parts.note: the is the definite article
It is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and It

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about a duty on Italian wine that has been abolished.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe was a tenth of produce paid to the Church, a levy since abolished.

clue.text: Discussion about foreign city displaying ancient vehicle (7)/td>

indicators.note: the chat word goes about, around, the city

parts.note: a chat is an informal discussion
Rio de Janeiro, a Brazilian city

explanation.surface: Talk of an overseas city brings up a vehicle from antiquity.
explanation.definitionFit: A chariot was a two-wheeled horse-drawn cart used in ancient warfare and racing.

clue.text: A prosecuting officer's girl

parts.note: a DA is a District Attorney, a US public prosecutor; the 's means is

explanation.surface: A lawyer's daughter.
explanation.definitionFit: Ada is a girl's name, the kind of name a clue calls a girl.

clue.text: Fiasco trying to accommodate race venue

indicators.note: the two words accommodate, house, the letters within them

explanation.surface: A disastrous attempt to find room for a racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: ASCOT is a famous English racecourse near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is the Berkshire racecourse that hosts Royal Ascot.

clue.text: Miss? Nice one, perhaps

definitions.meaning: a form of address for an unmarried woman
a young woman from Nice, the French city, addressed in French

explanation.surface: Praise for a near miss: nice one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' looks like the adjective but is the French city.
explanation.definitionFit: The French title for an unmarried woman equals the English title Miss, so a girl from Nice would be one.
